McHenry County sits in north central North Dakota. Towner is the county seat. The county includes small towns, farm areas, hunting land, fishing areas, and wildlife refuge land. This guide explains how McHenry County tax deed sales work. It covers sale timing, bidder rules, payment terms, buyer risks, OTC options, and due diligence steps. McHenry County posts foreclosed property updates through its county site.

What Is McHenry County Tax Deed Investing?

McHenry County sells property after unpaid taxes move through North Dakota tax deed rules. Investors do not buy tax lien certificates at this county sale. They bid on county held real estate. The county deed passes the county’s interest to the buyer. The buyer should still check title, access, use, and any liens that may survive.

Important Details

The county notice and state law show that McHenry County follows North Dakota tax deed sale rules. The annual sale begins on the third Tuesday in November. The county’s posted notices have used 9:00 AM as the sale time. McHenry County is in Central Time.

Key Takeaways

  • McHenry County offers tax deed sales, typically held on the third Tuesday of November, allowing investors to buy county-held properties directly.
  • Investors should conduct due diligence regarding title, access, and potential liens before bidding on properties.
  • The auction process includes checking posted lists, attending the auction or using a proxy, and paying immediately after winning a bid.
  • Investors can also buy unsold tax deeds through OTC purchases, which provide more control and less pressure than live auctions.
  • Local economic advantages, like strong agricultural ties and demand from nearby areas, make McHenry County appealing for tax deed investors.

Fun Facts About McHenry County

• McHenry County was named for James McHenry. He was an early settler tied to Vermillion, South Dakota.
• The county was formed from part of Bottineau County during territorial days.
• Towner remains the county seat.
• Census estimates place the county near 5,100 people.
• The county has 53 townships and 12 cities.

Attractions and Economic Highlights

• Attractions: J. Clark Salyer National Wildlife Refuge, Cottonwood Lake National Wildlife Refuge, and Wintering River National Wildlife Refuge.
• Transportation: US 2 and US 52 serve the area near key county routes.
• Economy: agriculture, cattle, natural resources, and tourism support the county.
• Community: hunting, fishing, birding, and small town living are strong local draws.

Why McHenry County Is Ideal for Tax Deed Investors

• McHenry County can offer state tax lien opportunities in a deed format.
• Low minimum bids may create high returns when research is strong.
• It can fit a low risk investment plan only after title and land checks.
• Small town lots may suit buy and hold plans.
• Rural parcels may appeal to land buyers, neighbors, and local users.

Auction Process for McHenry County Tax Deed Sales

McHenry County tax deed sales happen as public auctions. State law says annual sales begin on the third Tuesday in November. The county sells each parcel to the highest eligible bidder. The bid must meet the posted minimum sale price. The county can reject bids with county approval.

How the Auction Works

  1. Step 1: Check the posted list

    Review the legal description, city or township, and minimum bid.

  2. Step 2: Inspect before bidding

    The county tells buyers to check title, place, use, and condition before the sale.

  3. Step 3: Attend or send a proxy

    McHenry County says buyers must attend or have a representative present.

  4. Step 4: Bid at or above the minimum

    The property sells to the highest eligible bidder.

  5. Step 5: Pay right away

    The county terms call for cash or check deposited with the Treasurer right away.

  6. Step 6: Wait for the county deed

    The county sends the deed after county approval and recording steps.

Maximum Returns and Expected Returns on McHenry County Tax Deeds

McHenry County tax deeds do not pay a fixed interest rate like tax lien certificates. Your expected returns come from resale, rental use, neighbor sale, land use, or long term value. State law sets the minimum price around taxes, special assessments, penalties, interest, costs, and estimated current taxes. That can create room for a deal when the parcel has real demand.

According to our review, many McHenry County tax deed parcels can be small town lots, outlots, or vacant land. That means access, use, and title checks matter more than house repair math.

Open to All Investors and Foreign Investor Participation

The county rules I found do not list a citizenship limit. They do require the buyer to attend or use a proxy. They also say the winning bidder must not owe back taxes anywhere in North Dakota. Foreign buyers should call the Auditor before bidding. They should ask how to write the deed name, how to pay, and what tax forms the county needs.

Importance of Due Diligence in McHenry County Tax Deed Investing

Due diligence means checking the property before you bid. McHenry County makes no promise about title, condition, use, liens, easements, or property lines. The county also says some outside assessments may remain after sale. This is why cheap property can still cost money later.

What Due Diligence Entails

• Run a title search.
• Check taxes and special assessments.
• Visit the property from a public road.
• Confirm legal access.
• Check flood, code, and building rules.
• Ask about occupants before entry.
• Check recorded IRS liens.

Risks of Skipping Due Diligence

• You may buy land with no access.
• A survey may cost more than expected.
• A use limit may block your plan.
• Some liens or assessments may remain.
• A quiet title case may be needed before resale.

Buying OTC Tax Deeds in McHenry County

How to Purchase OTC Tax Deeds

North Dakota law allows unsold tax deed property to be sold between annual sales. The county auditor may sell unsold property by private sale before the next November sale. The price cannot be below the approved minimum sale price unless a lawful reappraisal or related action applies. Check McHenry County’s Foreclosed Property page and property list for current county held parcels.

Benefits of OTC Purchases

OTC purchases may have less bidding pressure. You can review the parcel before making an offer. You may also have more time to call the county, check maps, and speak with local contacts. The main benefit is control. You avoid the rush of the live tax deed sale.

Why McHenry County Is a Top Choice for Tax Deed Investors

Economic and Tax Advantages

• McHenry County has strong ties to agriculture and cattle.
• Natural resources and tourism also support local demand.
• The county’s low density can create land plays.
• Small towns may offer simple entry points.
• Nearby Minot area demand can help some buyer pools.

Real Estate Market Overview

Census data shows a high owner occupied home rate in McHenry County. It also reports a median owner occupied home value near $151,000. That does not mean every tax deed is a deal. It does show a real local housing base. Buyers should compare each minimum bid with nearby sales, use, repairs, and resale demand.

Conclusion

McHenry County, North Dakota tax deed sales give investors a way to buy county held property through public auction. The typical annual sale begins on the third Tuesday in November. The county has used 9:00 AM Central Time in its posted sale notices. Buyers must attend or use a proxy. Winning bidders pay right away with cash or check.

The best deals come from research. Check title, access, use, special assessments, and resale demand. Treat every parcel as its own project. Tax deed benefits can be strong, but smart investing starts before the auction.

Pro Tips

• Call the Auditor before the sale and ask if any parcels were removed.
• Compare town lots in Towner, Velva, Upham, Drake, and Anamoose with nearby assessed values.
• For rural parcels, check access and whether the land is part of an active farm lease.
• Ask the Treasurer if any special assessments may remain.
• For resale, speak with neighbors first. Nearby owners often understand the land best.

McHenry County Tax Deed FAQs

• Do I need quiet title after buying?

Many buyers use quiet title before resale or financing. Ask a North Dakota attorney.

• Can I enter the property right after winning?

Do not enter without legal right. Check occupancy first.

• Can I finance a tax deed buy?

Most buyers bring cash. Lenders may want clear title later.

• Can old liens survive?

Some interests may remain. Check IRS liens, easements, and assessments.

• Can I flip the property fast?

Maybe. Title issues, access, and buyer demand will decide.
